headline: Inflation holds at 3.1%; Carney meets Xi tonight; Ukraine hits Crimean bridge
briefing: Canada's inflation rate stayed at 3.1% in October, a little below forecasts, and economists now lean toward the Bank of Canada holding its rate on Dec. 9. Prime Minister Carney meets China's Xi Jinping late Monday evening Ontario time, after saying Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if U.S. trade talks fail. Oil is steady near US$96 after a tanker was hit leaving the Strait of Hormuz, and Ukraine struck the Crimean bridge in a record drone attack.

keyDates.label: Carney–Xi meeting; Nvidia results; Ukraine arms meeting
keyDates.why: Carney meets Xi in Shenzhen (late Monday evening in Ontario), Ukraine's military backers meet at NATO headquarters in Brussels, Nvidia reports results after markets close, Israel's parliament votes on a new speaker and Iran's foreign minister visits Oman.

keyDates.label: APEC summit opens; Alaska ranked-choice count
keyDates.why: Leaders meet in Shenzhen on Nov. 18–19, and Alaska tabulates its Peltola–Sullivan Senate race if no one tops 50%.

keyDates.label: Trump meets Xi and Putin
keyDates.why: Trump holds a one-on-one with Xi and then a first-ever three-way meeting with Xi and Putin in Shenzhen, with nuclear weapons the stated focus.

keyDates.label: Senate Democrats vote; Stelco recall
keyDates.why: Democratic senators choose between Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen for majority leader by secret ballot, and 175 laid-off Stelco workers are due back in Hamilton.

keyDates.label: Bank of Canada and Fed rate decisions
keyDates.why: Both central banks decide the same day; after October's flat inflation reading, economists lean toward a Bank of Canada hold.

keyDates.label: U.S. government funding deadline
keyDates.why: Federal funding runs out unless the outgoing Congress passes a spending bill or a temporary extension, which is also the likeliest vehicle for any new air traffic control money.

stories.headline: Inflation holds at 3.1% in October, below forecasts; economists lean toward a December rate hold
stories.summary: Statistics Canada said Monday that consumer prices rose 3.1% in October from a year earlier, the same pace as September and slightly under the 3.2% economists expected. Gasoline is still the main driver, while prices outside energy cooled a little.
stories.now: Gasoline prices were up 30.9% from a year earlier, compared with 27.8% in September, although they fell 2.5% from September to October; Statistics Canada said part of the larger annual gain reflects a drop in crude oil prices in October 2025. Leaving out energy, prices rose 2.0%, down from 2.1%, and leaving out both food and energy the rate slowed to 1.8%. Slower rent increases and cheaper cellphone plans held the overall figure down, while grocery prices rose 2.0%, picking up after four months of slower growth. In Ontario, natural gas prices were up 3% from a year earlier after an 18.7% drop in September. CIBC economist Andrew Grantham said the mild reading, lower gas prices and a weak job market mean the Bank of Canada has no need to rush another increase; Oxford Economics said a December hold is now more likely but still expects one more quarter-point hike before a long pause, and TD's Leslie Preston described October's hike as pre-emptive. Canada lost 4,700 jobs in October and unemployment rose to 6.7%.
stories.backstory: Oil prices jumped after the U.S.-Iran war disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz this year, and fuel costs have pushed up inflation since. Canada's annual rate rose to 3.1% in September, led by gasoline, while core measures stayed near 2%. On Oct. 28 the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate to 2.5%, its first increase in more than three years, and said more hikes were possible. Oil has since fallen from a late-October peak above US$117 to the mid-US$90s.

timeline.event: Inflation at 3.0%

stories.why: This was the last inflation reading before the Bank of Canada's Dec. 9 decision. With the headline rate flat and prices outside energy running at or below 2%, the report weakens the case for a second straight rate increase, though the central bank has not signalled its intentions.
stories.impact: If you have a variable-rate mortgage or line of credit, or a renewal coming up, a December hold would mean no further increase in payments for now. Gas remains far more expensive than a year ago, and Ontario households are also seeing natural gas bills rise again heading into winter.

stories.headline: Carney to meet Xi within hours after naming Chinese automakers as a fallback to a U.S. deal
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Tuesday morning local time, which is late Monday evening in Ontario. He says talks with Washington remain his priority, but Canada could turn to Chinese, European or Japanese carmakers if a deal fails to keep the North American auto industry integrated.
stories.now: Speaking to reporters in Phnom Penh before leaving for China, Carney said the outcome of the U.S. negotiations will decide whether Ottawa pursues auto partnerships elsewhere. Asked whether Chinese investment was a bargaining chip, he said it was not leverage but a matter of action and reaction. He said any Chinese investment would need real manufacturing in Canada rather than so-called kit plants that only assemble imported parts, and that limits on Chinese investment stay in place in areas he has previously listed as defence-related sectors, artificial intelligence and critical minerals. The National Observer reports the Xi meeting is a short one at the start of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, and the Globe and Mail quotes a source expecting further tariff-reduction announcements afterward; there are also hopes China will cut more of its tariffs on Canadian farm products. Canada is trying to persuade President Donald Trump to scale back 25% tariffs on Canadian-made vehicles, and Trump has threatened new auto tariffs starting in January. Ontario Premier Doug Ford and the union Unifor criticized January's deal that lowered Canada's tariff on a capped number of Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1% from 100%.
stories.backstory: The United States has imposed tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum, vehicles and other goods since 2025, and Canada answered with counter-tariffs plus relief programs for its own importers. Washington announced further tariffs on Canadian goods in July, and Canada pulled out of negotiations in the summer after last-minute U.S. demands. The North American trade pact known as CUSMA in Canada and USMCA in the United States is also under review. After Democrats won Congress on Nov. 3, Carney said the Trump administration is still the side Canada has to negotiate with.

stories.why: A deal with Washington would do more for the Canadian economy than any new agreement in Asia, because about three-quarters of Canada's exports go to the United States. Carney's condition signals that Ottawa would rather wait than accept terms that shrink auto assembly in Canada.
stories.impact: Ontario's auto plants and parts suppliers, including those in Brampton, Oakville, Oshawa, Alliston and Windsor, depend on tariff-free access to the U.S. market, so the terms on autos matter directly for jobs in the GTA. Until a deal is signed, existing tariffs and counter-tariffs stay in place, which keeps some vehicle, steel and consumer prices higher.

stories.headline: Oil holds near US$96 after tanker hit leaving the Strait of Hormuz; Iran's foreign minister heads to Oman
stories.summary: Oil prices were little changed on Monday after a British maritime agency said a tanker leaving the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an unknown projectile, starting an engine-room fire with no casualties reported. Iran's foreign minister is due in Oman, which has mediated in the crisis, on Tuesday.
stories.now: United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), a British navy-run agency that tracks threats to shipping, said the tanker was hit at about 05:58 GMT on Monday while sailing out of the strait and that all crew are accounted for; no one has claimed responsibility. Iran's navy and Revolutionary Guards separately said tankers struck mines, claims that have not been independently verified, and market reports say traders are largely discounting them. Trading reports through Monday put Brent crude between about US$95.40 and US$96.30 a barrel, close to Friday's US$95.84 settlement, with the U.S. benchmark, West Texas Intermediate, near US$88.40. On Sunday, Bahrain said it intercepted Iranian drones that the Guards said were aimed at a U.S. radar; the Guards claim to have destroyed it, which is disputed. CNBC reports Iran's foreign minister is to visit Oman on Tuesday for talks with his counterpart. No new U.S. strikes have been reported; President Trump, now travelling to Asia, is keeping the naval blockade of Iranian ports and has reportedly told advisers he may hold off on strikes unless provoked.
stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran choked traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened it but collapsed in July, and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Qatar gave Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25. Trump has said the war will end soon, one way or the other.

stories.why: Oil prices are the main driver of higher inflation in Canada and the U.S.; the October spike is why the Bank of Canada raised rates on Oct. 28.
stories.impact: Lower crude usually reaches GTA gas pumps within days, and this month's drop has eased fuel and delivery costs. Sunday night's calm opening suggests the Bahrain attack has not, so far, reversed that; a confirmed hit on U.S. forces or on tankers, or new U.S. strikes, could still push oil back up quickly.

stories.headline: More than 300 U.S. flights cancelled Monday morning as recovery continues; Duffy's US$50-billion ask awaits details
stories.summary: U.S. air travel is close to normal on Monday, with a little over 300 cancellations by 7 a.m. Eastern compared with roughly 2,300 on Sunday and more than 9,000 on Friday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has yet to explain publicly how his US$50-billion request to rebuild air traffic systems would be spent.
stories.now: Flight tracker FlightAware counted more than 300 U.S. cancellations as of 7 a.m. Eastern on Monday, a number that was slowly rising; American Airlines accounted for 144, regional carrier SkyWest 38 and JetBlue 30, according to ABC News. That compares with about 2,300 on Sunday, roughly 6,700 on Saturday and more than 9,000 on Friday, when the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) halted all departures from 3:54 p.m. to 8:15 p.m. Eastern. Duffy has traced the failure to a router at an FAA site in El Dorado, Arkansas, and a second in Texas that flooded the network with connection attempts; the routers' maker says its devices worked as designed, some air traffic controllers have disputed his account, and news reports say the root cause is still not established. Late Friday he raised an earlier US$30.1-billion request, which included US$10.1 billion for air traffic control modernization, US$2 billion for towers and US$18 billion for airport projects, to US$50 billion without explaining the difference, and he promised specifics on Monday. Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, point to US$12.5 billion approved in 2025, about one-third of it spent. FAA and Transportation Department officials were due to brief Congress on Monday. Air Canada cancelled about 250 flights on Friday, affecting roughly 27,000 passengers.
stories.backstory: A ground stop is an order that keeps aircraft from taking off; planes already in the air continue to their destinations. Nationwide stops are very rare: CTV reported that Friday's was only the second halt of all U.S. departures since the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks, the other being a January 2023 failure of a pilot-notification system. The FAA's telecommunications network has caused regional stoppages before, including one in the Minneapolis area in August. Canada's own air traffic system was not affected, and the Greater Toronto Airports Authority said Pearson's systems were working normally. The outage came a day after an unrelated Microsoft email failure, and officials have not linked the two.

stories.why: A single network fault stopped departures across the world's busiest aviation system for hours, which raises questions about the age and resilience of U.S. air traffic control equipment. The administration is using it to press Congress for modernization money, and officials have warned similar failures could recur without upgrades.
stories.impact: If you are flying between the GTA and the U.S. on Monday, check your flight with the airline before leaving for Pearson or Billy Bishop; most schedules should be back to normal, but some aircraft and crews may still be out of position and rebooked seats are scarce. Under Canada's air passenger rules, airlines must rebook or refund you when a flight is cancelled, though cash compensation generally does not apply to disruptions outside the airline's control.

stories.headline: Ottawa and Ontario still seeking Stellantis CEO meeting as Brampton plant sale clock runs
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday that his government is not satisfied with Stellantis's approach in Canada, and tied the future of the auto sector to trade talks with Washington. Ottawa and Ontario are still waiting to put their package to stop the Brampton plant sale to global chief executive Antonio Filosa.
stories.now: Speaking in Manila on Saturday, Carney said the government is in no way satisfied with the current situation or with what he called Stellantis's partial approach to its Canadian operations, and said Canada will not sign a U.S. trade deal that leaves the auto sector unviable. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Friday that Ottawa is still trying to find a way to prevent the sale to armoured-vehicle maker Roshel, working with Ontario and with Unifor, the union for more than 9,000 Stellantis workers in Canada; she described the offer as an aggressive package but gave no details of what is in it. Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli said the aim of meeting Filosa is to buy some time by getting the company to slow the sale down, and that the province has not advanced any money for Brampton so far; he said any support for the scenarios Unifor has proposed would come from Ontario's existing $2.5-billion auto support fund. No date for the Filosa meeting has been announced. Joly has said Ottawa cannot block the sale under the Investment Canada Act because the seller is a Canadian subsidiary, so its leverage is the subsidy agreement: up to $529 million was committed in 2022 for the Brampton and Windsor plants, and Stellantis has offered to return $24 million. The 30-day default period began Thursday, and Stellantis expects the sale to close by the end of the year.
stories.backstory: The Brampton plant built Dodge and Chrysler cars and has been idle for about three years while workers stayed on paid layoff. In May 2022 Ottawa agreed to give Stellantis $529 million to retool its Brampton and Windsor plants, and the company had planned to build the Jeep Compass in Brampton. In October 2025 it moved that vehicle to Illinois as U.S. tariffs on Canadian-made cars took hold. Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel in September, Unifor's contract expired Sept. 20, and the union declared an impasse over the plant's future.

stories.why: The sale ends hopes that a major GTA auto plant would restart vehicle production, and it tests whether governments can enforce the conditions attached to public subsidies. It also shows how U.S. tariffs are pulling auto investment out of Ontario.
stories.impact: Thousands of Peel Region families depend on the plant and its parts suppliers, and most laid-off workers have no guarantee of a job with the new owner. Taxpayers have a stake on both sides: any new support package would be public money, and the gap between the $24 million Stellantis has offered and what Ottawa says it is owed may end up in court.

stories.headline: Ukraine hits Crimean bridge in what Russia's figures show is the war's largest drone attack
stories.summary: Russia's Defence Ministry said it shot down 1,336 Ukrainian drones over 16 regions overnight into Monday, the most it has reported in a single attack since the 2022 invasion. The bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea was struck a day before Ukraine's arms donors meet in Brussels.
stories.now: The Russian tally tops the previous high of 1,254 drones reported on Oct. 29; such figures cannot be independently checked. Crimea's Russian-installed governor said the Kerch Bridge's road and rail span was hit, while Russia's Transport Ministry said trains kept running, and the Kremlin described the damage as minor. Officials said falling debris injured six people, including children, and the governor of the Rostov region reported fires at four industrial sites in the city of Azov. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said late Sunday that Ukrainian strikes have knocked out more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity, a claim Reuters said it could not verify. He also said Russia fired more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 guided bombs and 15 missiles at Ukraine over the past week. The attack follows U.S.-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi that ended without a breakthrough; U.S. envoy Jared Kushner says Washington is now trying to get Russia and European governments talking directly. The Ukraine Defence Contact Group, the allied arms-donor forum often called the Ramstein group, meets Tuesday at NATO headquarters in Brussels, where Zelenskyy wants missiles for Patriot and NASAMS air defence systems.
stories.backstory: U.S.-mediated efforts to end the war stalled for months while Washington focused on Iran. Rubio said in May that the effort had stagnated. Europe has repeatedly asked to be included in any deal affecting its own security.

stories.why: Linking NATO membership to land is a new idea in the talks and touches the two issues that have blocked a settlement: territory and Ukraine's long-term security. Any change to NATO's membership would need the agreement of all allies, including Canada.
stories.impact: Peace progress could ease energy and grain prices over time. Canada, a NATO and G7 member, would have a vote on any Ukrainian membership and would share in the security commitments that came with it.

stories.headline: Trump en route to Asia; Washington, Moscow and Beijing all confirm Thursday's three-way meeting
stories.summary: President Donald Trump left Washington on Monday for Manila and then Shenzhen, China, where he is to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin together on Thursday. The White House, the Kremlin and China's government have each confirmed the meeting, and U.S. officials say nuclear weapons are the focus.
stories.now: The White House schedule has Trump stopping in Anchorage, Alaska, and reaching Manila on Tuesday evening; Secretary of State Marco Rubio is travelling with him through Nov. 19. In the Philippines he is to meet President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., attend a meeting of the Quad (the United States, Japan, India and Australia), which would be his first with those leaders in this term, sign a U.S.-Thailand trade deal and dine with Southeast Asian leaders. In Shenzhen he attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' meeting and holds a one-on-one with Xi on Thursday, as the two countries' trade truce nears its expiry, before the three-way session with Putin, which U.S. officials call the first of its kind. Officials say there will be no separate Trump-Putin meeting and that they do not expect a nuclear arms agreement this week. CNN reports Trump plans to announce commercial deals and does not intend to raise the Nvidia spying allegations with Xi. Prime Minister Mark Carney meets Xi in Shenzhen on Tuesday.
stories.backstory: The trip comes two weeks after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and days after the head of chipmaker Nvidia resigned amid allegations that its chips reached a China-linked buyer. The United States is also still at war with Iran, and U.S.-brokered talks to end the war in Ukraine ended last week without a breakthrough. New START, the last treaty limiting U.S. and Russian nuclear arsenals, expired in February 2026. Some analysts quoted by Foreign Policy and the Council on Foreign Relations doubt the three-way meeting will produce much of substance.

stories.why: A joint meeting of the U.S., Chinese and Russian leaders has not happened before, and it could open talks on limiting nuclear weapons. It is also a test of Trump's standing abroad after a midterm defeat at home.
stories.impact: Trade between the U.S. and China shapes prices and supply chains for Ontario manufacturers, and Carney is pursuing his own talks with Xi at the same summit on Chinese auto investment. Any easing or worsening of U.S.-China tensions could affect Canada's room to make deals with both.

stories.headline: Tech stocks slide ahead of Nvidia's first results without Jensen Huang on Tuesday
stories.summary: U.S. stocks fell about 1% on Monday morning, led by technology shares, a day before Nvidia reports its first quarterly results since chief executive Jensen Huang resigned. Megaspeed, the Singapore-based chip buyer at the centre of the export scandal, has opened an internal probe.
stories.now: The Canadian Press reported the S&P 500 down 78.30 points at 7,483.37 during Monday trading, with Toronto's S&P/TSX composite index off more than 100 points; a market live blog had Nvidia down about 2.2% late in the morning. Nvidia reports after markets close on Tuesday, with a 5 p.m. Eastern call led by chief financial officer Colette Kress, the interim chief executive. Analysts expect revenue of roughly US$109 billion, against company guidance of US$108 billion plus or minus 2%, and earnings previews say options prices imply a swing of about 9% in either direction. Megaspeed said Sunday that former executive Alice Huang left the company on Aug. 30, 2025, and that it will cooperate with the U.S. investigation; it did not address the spying allegations reported about her, none of which have been proven. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that Nvidia should hire a chief executive from outside. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department oversees chip export controls, is to testify to the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10, and the White House says President Trump keeps confidence in him.
stories.backstory: Huang co-founded Nvidia and has run it since 1993, building it into the main supplier of the chips used to train artificial intelligence (AI) systems and one of the world's most valuable companies. Earlier this week, reports said the company had opened an internal investigation into whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort through a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing. Huang told staff in a company email that he had been unfaithful in his marriage. The stock had already slipped on that first report before Wednesday's news.

The spying allegation also raises national-security questions in Washington, which controls what chips the company may sell to China.
stories.impact: Most Canadian pension plans, index funds and RRSP or TFSA portfolios that track U.S. stocks hold Nvidia, so its swings show up in retirement savings here. Quarterly results expected Tuesday and the fight over who runs the company could bring more volatility this week.

stories.headline: Peltola claims victory in Alaska; race still uncalled ahead of Wednesday's ranked-choice count
stories.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign has declared victory in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, where she holds about 49.9% of first-choice votes to Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan's 46%. The Associated Press has not called the race, and a ranked-choice tabulation is set for Wednesday if no one tops 50%.
stories.now: Peltola's campaign said over the weekend that Sullivan has no mathematical path to win and that she will be elected once the remaining votes are counted. The Associated Press, which estimates about 97% of the vote is in, has not called the race, and news reports say Sullivan has not conceded or commented publicly on the count in recent days. Saturday's update from the Alaska Division of Elections added 4,290 ballots and left Peltola at 49.9% and Sullivan at 46%; Friday's count had her ahead by 10,412 votes. Overseas ballots can still arrive until Nov. 18, when a ranked-choice tabulation will redistribute the votes of trailing candidates if no one has passed 50%. An NBC News analysis says Sullivan cannot catch up through those transfers if he ends the first-choice count more than about 6,600 votes behind. A Peltola win would give Democrats 56 of 100 Senate seats. The AP has already called Alaska's governorship for Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who takes office Dec. 7. Alaska plans to certify results on Nov. 25, and Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress in January.
stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers since January 2025, and all 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate were on the ballot. More than 53 million Americans voted early. Tariffs and high gas prices tied to the Iran war weighed on Trump's approval, and recent polls gave Democrats an edge in most key Senate races. Courts also turned back a Trump administration bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots.

stories.impact: Canadian exporters are watching whether a Democratic Congress moves to limit tariffs, which could ease pressure on Ontario manufacturers over time; near-term tariffs stay in place unless the White House changes them.

stories.headline: Door-to-door mail ends today for about 18,000 north Etobicoke homes
stories.summary: Canada Post switches about 18,000 homes in north Etobicoke from door-to-door delivery to community mailboxes starting Monday, the first such change in Toronto. The rest of the GTA follows in stages through 2031.
stories.now: The change applies to homes with postal codes beginning M9V and M9W, Canada Post has confirmed. Letters and most parcels will go to a shared, locked community mailbox nearby, while oversized packages and items needing a signature will still come to the door or be held at a post office. A Rexdale letter carrier walked her last door-to-door route on Friday, according to a news report. Published schedules show Ajax, Pickering, Mississauga and Brampton switching between September and November 2027, with North York and most of downtown Toronto last, by September 2031. Canada Post says people who cannot get to a community mailbox can apply for accommodations such as a more accessible compartment or weekly home delivery; the postal workers' union and disability advocates say the change will be hard on some residents.
stories.backstory: Canada Post has lost money for years as letter volumes fall and parcel competition grows. In September 2025 the federal government lifted its freeze on community mailbox conversions and told the Crown corporation to move the roughly four million addresses that still get door-to-door delivery. Canada Post said in April 2026 that the national switch should take about five years. An earlier conversion program that began in 2014 was halted after public opposition and formally cancelled in 2018. Sept-Îles, Que., and Winnipeg were the first to switch under the new plan in October, with Etobicoke and the Moncton, N.B., area following in November.

timeline.event: Ottawa lifts freeze on community mailbox conversions

stories.why: This is the first Toronto neighbourhood to lose home delivery under a plan that will eventually reach every GTA address that still has it. Canada Post says serving a door costs about twice as much as serving a community mailbox.
stories.impact: If your postal code starts with M9V or M9W, your mail goes to a community mailbox from Monday; check the notice Canada Post sent for your mailbox location and keys. Elsewhere in the GTA nothing changes yet, but you can check your area's date on Canada Post's website and apply for an accommodation if mobility is an issue.

stories.headline: Ontario's bill to cap OSAP at private career colleges is expected at Queen's Park today
stories.summary: Legislation that would limit how fast OSAP-funded enrolment can grow at private career colleges, and cut off student aid for programs taught mainly online, is expected to be tabled Monday. Colleges Minister Nolan Quinn outlined it last Thursday.
stories.now: Quinn said the province found coordinated and sophisticated efforts to exploit the Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP), not just paperwork problems. The proposed law would cap growth in OSAP-funded enrolment at private institutions, make mostly-online programs ineligible, require career colleges to have a physical campus and restrict their ties to outside immigration and recruitment firms. It would also make private colleges liable for their students' loans, so the province can recover money more easily, and add new fines. The government has cited thousands of applications from the same internet address, final exams finished in about six minutes and outsiders doing students' coursework. Opposition parties dismissed it as a bill meant to protect the government that does nothing for students caught in the freeze on aid at career colleges, which began in early October and remains in place; the Liberals want funding restored at schools with no evidence of wrongdoing. Quinn has said the province is working with banks on low-interest loans for affected students until the pause is lifted in the new year.
stories.backstory: OSAP is Ontario's student loan and grant program. Online programs at private career colleges became eligible during the pandemic, and spending there grew quickly: seven career colleges accounted for about $385 million in grants in 2024-25, roughly as much as all of Ontario's public colleges combined. The province barred several schools over the summer, then paused OSAP payments to all private post-secondary institutions while the accounting firm KPMG audits the sector; early findings were sent to the Ontario Provincial Police and the auditor general. Separately, thousands of students walked out on Nov. 5 over wider OSAP and tuition changes.

timeline.event: Five career colleges made ineligible for OSAP

stories.why: The province is trying to stop alleged large-scale misuse of public student aid without shutting out legitimate schools. How quickly it restarts payments decides whether thousands of students can continue their programs.
stories.impact: Students at private career colleges in the GTA still have no date for aid to resume, and those in mostly-online programs may lose eligibility altogether. Anyone enrolling should confirm a school's OSAP status before paying fees.

stories.headline: Carney leaves Francophonie summit for Shenzhen, where he meets Xi on Tuesday
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney wrapped up the summit of French-speaking countries in Phnom Penh on Monday and heads to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' meeting. He meets President Xi Jinping on Tuesday morning local time, late Monday evening in Ontario.
stories.now: Carney has said he expects to discuss the evolution of the international system, China's role in it and Canadian priorities, along with tariffs, trade and Chinese investment in the auto sector. The Globe and Mail has reported he also plans to tell Xi that foreign governments should not interfere in Canadian affairs. He told reporters in Phnom Penh on Monday that Ottawa has set clear guardrails on where it will work with China. On Sunday he held his first formal meeting with Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, whose Parti Québécois government favours independence; reports put it at 30 to 45 minutes, and the two agreed to cooperate on homelessness and to speak regularly, including on U.S. matters, with immigration, housing and the Alto high-speed rail project left for a second meeting. The premier defended letters he sent to nearly 60 U.S. elected officials after the midterms. On Saturday in Manila, Canada and the Philippines closed negotiations on a free trade agreement that Carney said could help triple two-way trade to more than $10 billion a year by 2035, with signing targeted for 2027.
stories.backstory: Canada and the Philippines first discussed a trade agreement in 2015, and Carney and Marcos agreed in October 2025 to restart and speed up the talks, alongside a separate Canada-ASEAN negotiation. The push is part of Ottawa's effort to find customers beyond the United States as tariffs from the Trump administration hit Canadian exports. The Asia trip also takes Carney to China, where he has said he will raise foreign interference with Xi; a federal public inquiry found China was the most active foreign state trying to interfere in Canadian democratic institutions. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has criticized the travel, saying the economy is about people struggling to make ends meet rather than summits. In Quebec, St-Pierre Plamondon leads a minority Parti Québécois government that has promised a third sovereignty referendum; reports differ on whether the target is 2029 or 2030.

timeline.event: Carney meets European leaders in Dublin, then leaves for Asia
Canada and the Philippines announce negotiations are concluded; Ottawa says ASEAN talks substantially concluded
Carney and Quebec's premier hold first meeting in Phnom Penh; agree to regular contact
Carney to meet Xi in Shenzhen at the start of the APEC summit
Target for signing the Canada-Philippines agreement

stories.why: The trip is meant to show Canada can rely less on the United States for trade, and the Philippines announcement is its first concrete result, though neither agreement is signed or in force. The Cambodia stop adds a domestic test: how Ottawa and a Quebec government committed to a future sovereignty referendum will work together.
stories.impact: Nothing changes at the border yet, so prices and tariffs stay as they are until the agreement is signed and ratified, likely not before 2027. The Philippines is one of the largest sources of new immigrants to the GTA, so lower barriers could eventually matter for local importers, food businesses and Ontario exporters, including pork producers.

stories.headline: Knesset to vote Tuesday on replacing its speaker as Eisenkot-Netanyahu talks stay deadlocked
stories.summary: Israel's parliament votes Tuesday at 4 p.m. local time on replacing Speaker Amir Ohana with Matan Kahana of Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party, after 67 of 120 lawmakers signed a request. Unity talks between Yashar and Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud have produced no agreement.
stories.now: Likud was represented by Knesset member Ofir Katz and Michael Rabello, a former personal lawyer to Netanyahu, and Yashar by Knesset member Chili Tropper and Yoav Horowitz. Both sides described the meeting as businesslike and said dialogue will continue. Yashar denied an Army Radio report that it had offered to rotate the premiership, saying its only proposal is for Likud to join a government led by Eisenkot; Netanyahu has said he should lead any unity government and wants his current allies included. Israel's Channel 12 reported that the session produced no progress, and the head of the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party denied reports of significant progress in its own contacts with Eisenkot's bloc. The next test is Tuesday's vote on making Yashar's Matan Kahana speaker of the Knesset in place of Likud's Amir Ohana, scheduled after 67 lawmakers signed a request; Netanyahu is pressing United Torah Judaism to oppose it, and control of the speaker's chair would let his opponents advance legislation while he governs as caretaker. Eisenkot, who called off an earlier round on Nov. 10 over a speech Netanyahu gave in parliament, has until Dec. 6 to assemble a majority, and the president can extend that by up to 14 days. Separately, an Israeli strike on Saturday in southern Gaza killed Samir Abu Younis, commander of Hamas's Rafah brigade, which both Hamas and Israel's military confirmed despite the ceasefire in place since October 2025.
stories.backstory: Israel voted on Oct. 27 and neither Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc nor the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot, a former army chief, won 61 of the 120 seats in the Knesset (parliament). President Isaac Herzog gave Eisenkot the first try at forming a government on Nov. 7 after parties holding 67 seats recommended him, against 46 for Netanyahu. Eisenkot has said he will not serve under Netanyahu, who remains caretaker prime minister. If no one can form a government, Israel faces another election.

timeline.event: Israel votes; no bloc wins 61 seats

stories.why: Who leads Israel affects the course of the war with Iran, the Gaza ceasefire and relations with Washington. The coalition arithmetic remains difficult for both men.
stories.impact: Effects on Ontario are indirect: regional stability feeds into oil and gasoline prices, and Toronto's large Jewish, Israeli and Palestinian communities follow these events closely.

stories.headline: Russia out of world juniors in Alberta after Canada refuses entry; Moscow appeals to IOC
stories.summary: The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) confirmed Sunday that Russia will not play at the world junior championship in Edmonton and Red Deer because the Canadian government will not let the team in. Russia's hockey federation calls the decision unlawful and says it will appeal to the International Olympic Committee (IOC).
stories.now: The IIHF said it looked at alternative arrangements but decided Canada will stay as host of the tournament, which runs Dec. 26 to Jan. 5. Ottawa has said it opposes Russian and Belarusian participation as long as Russia's war on Ukraine continues, and officials clarified that even Russian players holding valid visas would be barred from the event; the government welcomed the IIHF decision and said its position will not change. Russia's federation said it will appeal to the IOC and may seek compensation, and Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyaryov said the tournament should be moved out of Canada. Separately, the hockey federations of Norway, Denmark, Sweden and the Czech Republic have said their teams will refuse to play Russia at next year's men's world championship in Germany.
stories.backstory: Russia and Belarus have been shut out of IIHF tournaments since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Late last month the Court of Arbitration for Sport, the top tribunal for international sports disputes, ruled that Russia must be reinstated to international hockey. Canada, the host of this winter's under-20 championship, responded that it would not admit the Russian team.

timeline.event: IIHF suspends Russia and Belarus after the invasion of Ukraine
Court of Arbitration for Sport orders Russia reinstated to international hockey
IIHF confirms Russia will miss the world juniors; Canada stays host
World junior championship opens in Edmonton and Red Deer

stories.why: It is a direct clash between a sports court ruling and a host government's foreign policy, and it could spill into other tournaments as more countries refuse to play Russia.
stories.impact: For Ontario hockey fans, the tournament goes ahead in Alberta as scheduled over the holidays, without Russia. Ticket holders and viewers should see no change to Canada's games unless an appeal forces one.
